intro: Six matriculation-exam-style problems bring together the quantity of heat, changes of state, thermal balance, thermal expansion and heat transfer from this lesson. Solve them as in the exam: say where the energy goes, solve for the quantity asked before substituting numbers, and assess whether the result is reasonable. Open the model answer and the marking scheme only when your solution is ready.

tasks.title: New ice for the ice rink
tasks.source_note: The rink and its numbers are invented examples. The thickness of the sprayed water layer and the cooling power have the same order of magnitude as the values of an ordinary ice rink.
tasks.text:
After the summer break new ice is made on the rink of an ice hall. Water is sprayed in thin layers on the cooled concrete slab, a layer of $3.00\,\text{cm}$ in all, which freezes over the whole area. The refrigeration machine of the hall removes heat from the water and ice at a power of $350\,\text{kW}$.

- area to be frozen $1800\,\text{m}^2$
- temperature of the water in the hose $15.0\,{}^\circ\text{C}$, temperature of the finished ice $-4.0\,{}^\circ\text{C}$
- density of water $1000\,\text{kg/m}^3$, for water $c = 4190\,\text{J/(kg}\cdot\text{K)}$, for ice $c = 2100\,\text{J/(kg}\cdot\text{K)}$, specific latent heat of fusion of ice $334\,\text{kJ/kg}$

The ice master says: "Once the water has cooled to zero degrees, freezing goes quickly, because the temperature no longer has to be lowered."

parts.text: At least how much heat must the refrigeration machine remove for all the water to become ice at $-4.0\,{}^\circ\text{C}$?

criteria.text: Divides the process into three stages: the water cools to $0\,{}^\circ\text{C}$, freezes at constant temperature, and the ice cools to $-4.0\,{}^\circ\text{C}$.

criteria.detail: $m = \rho A d$ and $Q = c_\text{w} m \Delta T_\text{w} + s m + c_\text{i} m \Delta T_\text{i}$
$m = 54\,000\,\text{kg}$; stages $3.39\,\text{GJ}$, $18.0\,\text{GJ}$ and $0.454\,\text{GJ}$; centimetres converted to metres by substitution.
$Q \approx 21.9\,\text{GJ}$ to three significant figures

parts.text: At least how long does the freezing take?

criteria.detail: $t = \dfrac{Q}{P}$
about $17.4\,\text{h}$
The real time is longer, because the refrigeration machine also removes heat conducted from the air of the hall and from the concrete; the result is a lower limit.

parts.text: Assess the ice master's claim with the results of part a.

criteria.text: Calculates the shares of the stages: freezing about $82\,\%$, cooling of the water about $16\,\%$ and cooling of the ice about $2\,\%$ of the total heat.

Explains that freezing releases the latent heat of fusion $sm$, which must be removed although the temperature stays at $0\,{}^\circ\text{C}$; in freezing the interaction energy of the particles decreases.
Compares as times: cooling the water takes about $2.7\,\text{h}$, freezing about $14\,\text{h}$.

criteria.detail: The claim is wrong: freezing is the slowest stage of the process.

tasks.title: Heat-storing fireplace
tasks.source_note: The house and the fireplace are invented examples. The specific heat capacity of soapstone, about $980\,\text{J/(kg}\cdot\text{K)}$, and the heat of combustion of air-dried birch logs, about $15\,\text{MJ/kg}$, are typical rounded values.
tasks.text:
A detached house has a heat-storing fireplace built of soapstone. In the evenings $12.0\,\text{kg}$ of air-dried birch logs are burnt in it, and when the fire has gone out the damper is closed. The stone mass gives out heat to the rooms during the next day and cools back to its initial temperature.

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| stone mass | $1800\,\text{kg}$ |
| $c$ of soapstone | $980\,\text{J/(kg}\cdot\text{K)}$ |
| heat of combustion of birch | $15\,\text{MJ/kg}$ |
| share transferred to the stone | $80\,\%$ |

The house loses heat through the walls, windows, roof and ventilation at $150\,\text{W}$ in all for every kelvin of difference between the indoor and outdoor temperatures. The indoor temperature is kept at $21\,{}^\circ\text{C}$.

parts.text: By how much does the average temperature of the stone mass rise during one firing?

criteria.detail: $Q = \eta H m_\text{wood}$ and $\Delta T = \dfrac{Q}{c\,m_\text{stone}}$
$Q = 0.80 \cdot 15\,\text{MJ/kg} \cdot 12.0\,\text{kg} = 144\,\text{MJ}$; megajoules converted to joules.
$\Delta T \approx 82\,\text{K}$ to two significant figures like the heat of combustion and the share
The temperature of the stone mass is not uniform: the inner parts warm up more and the surface less, so the result is an average.

parts.text: At what average power does the fireplace heat the house during the next day?

criteria.detail: $P = \dfrac{Q}{t}$, where $t = 24\,\text{h}$
$P = 144 \cdot 10^{6}\,\text{J} : 86\,400\,\text{s}$; hours converted to seconds.
$P \approx 1.7\,\text{kW}$

parts.text: The mean temperature of a frosty day is $-10\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. What share of the heat demand of the house does the fireplace cover?

criteria.detail: Loss power $P_\text{loss} = 150\,\tfrac{\text{W}}{\text{K}} \cdot \Delta T$, and in energy balance the heating power equals the loss power.
$\Delta T = 21\,{}^\circ\text{C} - (-10\,{}^\circ\text{C}) = 31\,\text{K}$ and $P_\text{loss} = 4650\,\text{W}$; share $1667\,\text{W} : 4650\,\text{W}$.

parts.text: The neighbour's thin-walled sheet-metal stove warms up quickly, but the room cools soon after the fire goes out. Explain the difference from the heat-storing fireplace.

criteria.text: Explains with the heat capacity $C = cm$: the large stone mass stores the same energy with a small rise in temperature, while the thin sheet metal gets hot but stores little.
Links the temperature difference to power: the hot surface of the stove gives out the energy quickly at a high power, the moderately warm surface of the fireplace slowly over the whole day.

criteria.detail: The fireplace evens out the heating over time: the same fuel energy is spread more evenly, and the room stays warm after the fire has gone out.

tasks.title: Vaporisation of boiling water
tasks.source_note: The data are an invented example: the numbers have been calculated from a model in which the specific latent heat of vaporisation is $2.26\,\text{MJ/kg}$ and about $70\,\text{W}$ of heat is conducted from the container to the room regardless of the power, and variation like that of real measurements has been added to them.
tasks.text:
A group determined the specific latent heat of vaporisation of water. An open steel container of water stood on a balance, and in the water there was an immersion heater whose power could be adjusted. When the water was boiling steadily, the group read the change $\Delta m$ in the reading of the balance over five minutes ($300\,\text{s}$). The measurement was repeated at five powers $P$.

| $P\ (\text{W})$ | $\Delta m\ (\text{g})$ |
|---|---|
| $200$ | $17.9$ |
| $400$ | $43.1$ |
| $600$ | $70.8$ |
| $800$ | $96.4$ |
| $1000$ | $123.8$ |

A member of the group calculated the result from the $600\,\text{W}$ measurement alone: $r = \dfrac{P\,t}{\Delta m} \approx 2.54\,\text{MJ/kg}$.

parts.text: Draw a graph of the mass of water vaporised as a function of the power of the heater, and fit a suitable model to the points.

criteria.detail: $P\ (\text{W})$ on the horizontal axis, $\Delta m\ (\text{g})$ on the vertical axis, the scales start from zero.
A rising straight line is fitted to the points, passing between them; the line is not forced through the origin.

criteria.text: Extends the line as a dashed line to the horizontal axis for part c.

parts.text: Determine the specific latent heat of vaporisation of water with the help of the graph.

criteria.detail: The slope from two points of the line far apart, for example $(100\,\text{W};\ 4.0\,\text{g})$ and $(1100\,\text{W};\ 137.0\,\text{g})$: about $0.133\,\text{g/W}$.

criteria.text: Justifies the model: energy is conserved, so $(P - P_\text{loss})\,t = r\,\Delta m$, and the slope of the line is $\dfrac{t}{r}$.

criteria.detail: $r = \dfrac{t}{k} = \dfrac{300\,\text{s}}{0.133 \cdot 10^{-3}\,\text{kg/W}}$
$r \approx 2.26\,\text{MJ/kg}$; a result of $2.2$–$2.3\,\text{MJ/kg}$ is accepted.

parts.text: The line does not pass through the origin. Determine from the graph at what power the water would not vaporise at all, and interpret the result.

criteria.detail: The line crosses the horizontal axis at a power of about $70\,\text{W}$; $50$–$90\,\text{W}$ is accepted.

criteria.text: Interprets the intercept: part of the power of the heater is conducted through the walls and the surface of the container to the room and does not vaporise water; the loss power is about $70\,\text{W}$.

criteria.detail: $P_\text{loss} \approx 70\,\text{W}$ to one or two significant figures

parts.text: Assess why the value $2.54\,\text{MJ/kg}$ calculated from one measurement differs from the result of the graph, and which result is more reliable.

criteria.detail: The calculation from one measurement assumes that all the power goes into vaporisation, although about $70\,\text{W}$ is conducted to the room. The energy is then overestimated, and the result is too large, by about $12\,\%$.
The slope of the graph is more reliable: a constant loss only shifts the line and does not change the slope, and five points reduce the effect of random error.

The method assumes that the loss power is the same at all powers; this is justified, because boiling water is always at $100\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ and the temperature difference to the room stays the same.

tasks.title: A lake in winter
tasks.source_note: The situation is an invented example. The ice fisher's claim is an invented everyday belief that the problem assesses.
tasks.text:
A deep lake freezes in November. In late winter the ice is $40\,\text{cm}$ thick, but at the bottom of the lake the water is still at about $4\,{}^\circ\text{C}$, and the fish live there all winter. The upper surface of the ice is at the temperature of the frost and the lower surface at $0\,{}^\circ\text{C}$.

An ice fisher says: "A thick layer of snow on the ice strengthens the ice, because snow is cold and cools the ice."

parts.text: Explain why a lake freezes from the surface down and why there is water at about $4\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ at the bottom even in winter.

criteria.text: States that the density of water is greatest at about $4\,{}^\circ\text{C}$: between $0\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ and $4\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ water contracts as it warms.

Explains the layering: in autumn the cooling surface water sinks to the bottom until the whole lake is at about $4\,{}^\circ\text{C}$; after that the colder and lighter water stays at the surface and freezes.

criteria.detail: The water at $4\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ at the bottom is the densest, so it stays down under the ice.

parts.text: Explain with conservation of energy and heat transfer where the energy of the freezing water goes and why the ice grows more slowly the thicker it is.

criteria.text: States that when water freezes it gives out the latent heat of fusion, about $334\,\text{kJ}$ per kilogram, although the temperature stays at $0\,{}^\circ\text{C}$.
Explains that this energy is conducted through the ice to the cold air; the ice grows only as fast as the energy is conducted away.
Justifies that for the same temperature difference a smaller power is conducted through a thick layer of ice (a thicker layer has a smaller U-value), so ice forms more slowly.

parts.text: Assess the ice fisher's claim.

criteria.text: Notes that snow is a poor conductor of heat, because it contains a lot of air: it insulates the ice from the frost and does not cool it.
Concludes that under snow less energy is conducted away from the lower surface of the ice, so the ice grows more slowly and stays thinner.

criteria.detail: The claim is wrong: a snow cover slows down the growth of the ice. In addition, heavy snow can press the ice down, so that water rises on top of the ice and weak slush ice forms.

tasks.title: Heat of fusion of ice with a calorimeter
tasks.source_note: The report and its measurements are invented examples.
tasks.text:
An extract from a student group's report:

> We poured $0.200\,\text{kg}$ of water at $40.0\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ into a polystyrene cup. We took ice cubes from the freezer, weighed them quickly ($0.0500\,\text{kg}$) and dropped them into the water. We stirred until the ice had melted, and the temperature settled at $14.3\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. We calculated the specific latent heat of fusion of ice to be $371\,\text{kJ/kg}$. So the table value $334\,\text{kJ/kg}$ is wrong, or the cup takes heat.

The temperature of the freezer was $-18.0\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. For water $c = 4190\,\text{J/(kg}\cdot\text{K)}$ and for ice $c = 2100\,\text{J/(kg}\cdot\text{K)}$.

parts.text: Show how the group got the result $371\,\text{kJ/kg}$. What did the group assume about the initial temperature of the ice?

criteria.detail: $c_\text{w} m_\text{w} (T_\text{w} - T) = s m_\text{i} + c_\text{w} m_\text{i} T$, solved for $s$
Given out by the water $21\,537\,\text{J}$ and warming of the meltwater $2996\,\text{J}$; $s = 18\,541\,\text{J} : 0.0500\,\text{kg}$

criteria.text: States that the calculation assumes the ice was at $0\,{}^\circ\text{C}$, because the warming of the ice has not been taken into account.

parts.text: Calculate the result again taking into account the real initial temperature of the ice. Assess the group's conclusion.

criteria.detail: The warming of the ice $c_\text{i} m_\text{i} \cdot 18.0\,\text{K}$ is added to the energy balance.
$c_\text{i} m_\text{i} \Delta T_\text{i} = 1890\,\text{J}$ and $s = (18\,541 - 1890)\,\text{J} : 0.0500\,\text{kg}$
$s \approx 333\,\text{kJ/kg}$, three significant figures

The conclusion does not hold: the corrected result agrees with the table value, and the difference came from a wrong assumption, not from the table. The cup does not explain the difference: it would have to take about $1890\,\text{J}$, but the heat capacity of a polystyrene cup is only a few $\text{J/K}$.

parts.text: The group wants to repeat the measurement more reliably. Suggest three improvements and justify which source of error each one affects.

criteria.text: Uses ice that is melting at $0\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ and dries its surface before weighing, or measures the temperature of the ice and takes it into account (warming of the ice, water on the surface of the ice).
Determines the mass of the ice as a difference by weighing the cup before and after adding the ice, so that ice that melted or fell during handling does not distort the mass.
Reduces heat exchange with the surroundings: a lid, an initial temperature as far above room temperature as the final temperature is below it, or taking the heat capacity of the cup into account.

criteria.detail: Repeats the measurement several times and reports the mean and the spread of the results.

tasks.title: Brakes on a fell road
tasks.source_note: The car, the road and the numbers are invented examples. The share $85\,\%$ transferred to the brake discs and the driving resistance $450\,\text{N}$ are rounded order-of-magnitude values.
tasks.text:
The mass of a car with its passengers is $1600\,\text{kg}$. The total mass of the car's four cast-iron brake discs is $30\,\text{kg}$, and the specific heat capacity of iron is $450\,\text{J/(kg}\cdot\text{K)}$. When braking, about $85\,\%$ of the energy transferred to the brakes heats the discs and the rest the brake pads.

A fell road descends $250\,\text{m}$ over a distance of $4.0\,\text{km}$. The driver goes down the hill at a constant speed of $60\,\text{km/h}$ using only the brakes. Air resistance and rolling resistance brake the car with a total average force of $450\,\text{N}$.

parts.text: The car is stopped on a level road from a speed of $90\,\text{km/h}$. By how much does the temperature of the brake discs rise?

criteria.detail: $E_\text{k} = \tfrac{1}{2} m v^2$ and $0.85\,E_\text{k} = c\,m_\text{discs}\,\Delta T$
$90\,\text{km/h} = 90 \cdot \dfrac{1000\,\text{m}}{3600\,\text{s}} = 25\,\text{m/s}$ and $E_\text{k} = 500\,\text{kJ}$
$\Delta T \approx 31\,\text{K}$

parts.text: By how much would the temperature of the brake discs rise on the downhill if the discs gave out no heat to the air?

criteria.text: Justifies with the work–energy principle: the speed is constant, so the kinetic energy does not change, and the decrease in potential energy goes into the work of the driving resistances and into the brakes.

criteria.detail: $Q_\text{brakes} = mgh - F s$ and $\Delta T = \dfrac{0.85\,Q_\text{brakes}}{c\,m_\text{discs}}$
$mgh = 3.92\,\text{MJ}$, $Fs = 1.80\,\text{MJ}$ and to the discs $1.81\,\text{MJ}$
$\Delta T \approx 130\,\text{K}$ to two significant figures

parts.text: At the bottom of the hill the temperature of the discs was measured to have risen by only $80\,\text{K}$. What share of the energy that came into the discs was transferred to the air during the descent, and in which ways was it transferred?

criteria.detail: $c\,m\,\Delta T = 1.08\,\text{MJ}$ stayed in the discs, $1.81\,\text{MJ} - 1.08\,\text{MJ} \approx 0.73\,\text{MJ}$ was transferred to the air.

criteria.text: Names the modes of transfer: mainly convection to the air flowing past the disc, in addition thermal radiation and conduction through the hub and the rim.

parts.text: The driver is advised: "On a long downhill use engine braking, so that the brakes do not overheat." Justify the advice using energy.

criteria.text: Explains that in engine braking the potential energy turns, through the friction of the engine, into internal energy in the engine, and the engine's cooling system gives it out to the air.

criteria.detail: The brake discs stay cooler and the braking power is kept for when the brakes are needed; the energy does not disappear, but the body it heats changes.
